info.bio:
Rancid es una banda de punk rock y ska americana, formada en 1991 en Berkeley, California, encabezaron el resurgimiento del punk tras los años 1980.

El estilo de Rancid pasa del punk y el hardcore por el ska, el reggae, el rocksteady, y algunas de rub-a-dub y funk. Entre el gran público, Rancid es conocido por las canciones "Ruby Soho" y "Time Bomb" del disco de 1995 ...And Out Come the Wolves.

Sus canciones tratan de los malos tiempos ("7 Years Down"

scenes.name: Hardcore en la era del punk-pop: emocore, ska-core y post-hardcore
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Mientras las revistas anuncian la «muerte del punk», el hardcore se convierte en un movimiento que no deja pueblo sin tocar y genera subgéneros. El «emocore» (Jawbreaker, Weezer, Sunny Day Real Estate, Promise Ring, At The Drive-In, Jimmy Eat World, Seaweed); el hardcore progresivo de Washington (Nation Of Ulysses, Make-Up, Shudder To Think, Jawbox, Edsel, Lungfish, Circus Lupus, Dismemberment Plan); el «ska-core» (Operation Ivy, Rancid, Mighty Mighty Bosstones, Sublime, No Doubt); el punk-pop que llega a las listas (Green Day, Offspring, Flop, Pennywise, Pegboy, Superchunk, Queers); el garage-punk californiano (Drive Like Jehu, Rocket From The Crypt, Blink 182, Zen Guerrilla); el jazzcore (Bazooka, Iceburn); la vieja escuela (D Generation, Supersuckers, Zeke, Dropkick Murphys, Silverfish, Turbonegro) y el post-hardcore de Unwound.

Their guitarist, Tim "Lint" Armstrong, formed Rancid (1), and proceeded to sell the idea to the masses. Rancid (1993) and especially Let's Go (1994) disguised the rebellious spirit of hardcore under the appearance of exuberant wit, irresistible rhythms and…

podcast.title: Accusations of Selling Out
podcast.body: As Rancid gained popularity and commercial recognition, they, alongside other successful pop punk bands like Green Day and The Offspring, were accused of "selling out" by punk purists. "purists became annoyed, accusing groups like Green Dan, the offspring and Rancidov selling out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Band Origins and Label Strategy
podcast.body: Rancid evolved from the revered band Operation Ivy and were label-mates with Bad Religion on Epitaph. Their songs were known for being short, tight, and melodic, perfectly complementing the sound kids sought after Green Day's success. They balanced punk ethics with commercial reach by remaining on Epitaph while securing distribution and quiet promotion from Warner Brothers. "Not only was Ransett label-mates with bad religion, but they devolved out of a band called Operation Ivy, a group that was revered by a young Billy Joe Armstrong, who of course was in Green Day"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Clash-like Sound
podcast.body: This band was noted for sometimes sounding more like The Clash than The Clash themselves. "Ransett, who sometimes sounded more clash than the clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaboration with Pink
podcast.body: Tim Armstrong, the frontman for this Bay Area punk band, produced and co-wrote two-thirds of Pink's third album, "Try This," released in 2003. This collaboration marked a significant shift for Pink into a harder rock sound. "Tim Armstrong, frontman for the Bay Area punk band, Rancid, produced and co-wrote two-thirds of Try This."

Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Commitment to Indie Label
podcast.body: Unlike Green Day, Rancid opted to remain an independent band, recording their music for Epitaph Records, the label founded by members of Bad Religion. "But unlike Green Day, Ranset chose to stay indie, recording for Bad Religion's Epitaph Records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Connecting Fans to Original Punk
podcast.body: Through Rancid's influence, many younger fans were introduced to the original British punk bands of the 1970s, such as The Clash. This connection also led to a resurgence of previously out-of-fashion styles, like big spiky mohawks, at Rancid's shows. "And through Ranset, a lot of kids were led back to the original British punks of the 1970s, like the clash. Big spiky mohawks were seen at a lot of Ranset shows, something that had gone out of fashion for a while."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dual Revival Role
podcast.body: Rancid descended from the hardcore punk band Operation Ivy, which had started incorporating Ska as early as 1987. Rancid figured prominently in both the punk revival and the third wave of Ska, benefiting from the growing popularity of punk revivalists like Green Day and The Offspring. "Then came Ranset, who figured in both the punk revival and third wave SCAT. And as punk revivalists like Green Day and the offspring got bigger and bigger, Ranset was basically sucked up in their wake."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Elder Statesmen of the Scene
podcast.body: With some members approaching 30, Rancid was perceived as the "older brothers" or "elder statesmen" of the mid-90s punk scene, which garnered them a certain level of respect among younger fans. "Ranset were a little older too, with a couple of members pushing 30. They were seen as the older brothers, the elder statesmen of the scene, and that brought them a certain amount of respect."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Evolution from Operation Ivy
podcast.body: Rancid formed and evolved from Operation Ivy, a Bay Area band that preceded them in the punk scene. "They evolved out of a Bay Area band called Operation Ivy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Fourth Wave Continuation
podcast.body: Rancid is mentioned as a third-wave group that is finding new fans, indicating their continued relevance and contribution to the emergence of the fourth wave of Ska. "Third wave groups like Ranset and Wheel Big Fish are finding new fans."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Hellcat Records Association
podcast.body: The label Hellcat Records, which records The Interrupters, is associated with Rancid, highlighting the band's ongoing influence in the Ska scene. "They're from Los Angeles and record for Hellcat Records, a label associated with, and here's that name again, Ranset."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Mainstream Exposure via MTV
podcast.body: Despite being an indie band, Rancid was propelled into the mainstream "stratosphere" due to the immense popularity created by Green Day. MTV, searching for more songs similar to Green Day's hits, discovered Rancid and their song "Salvation," giving them significant exposure. "But because of the huge vortex formed around Green Day, Ranset was sucked up into the stratosphere anyway, thanks largely to MTV. They went looking for more songs like Basket Case and Longview, and that's when they found Ranset and Salvation."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Melodic Enough for Prime Time
podcast.body: Rancid was identified as a "pure punk band" whose melodic qualities made them suitable for broader mainstream exposure. This characteristic helped them appeal to a wider audience beyond traditional punk circles. "Another pure punk band that was deemed melodic enough for prime time was Rancid."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Multiple Warped Tour Appearances
podcast.body: Rancid has agreed to participate in the Warped Tour at least three times. "Ransid has agreed to participate at least three times."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origins and Green Day's Support
podcast.body: Rancid, a Bay Area band, formed in 1991 following the disbandment of Operation Ivy, which Green Day members Billy Joe Armstrong and Mike Dirnt had been big fans of. As Green Day gained prominence, they actively promoted Rancid, drawing them into the mainstream spotlight. "Ranset came together in 1991 once Op Ivy disbanded after a couple of years, and as Green Day was blowing up, they chatted up Ranset whenever they could."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Tim Armstrong's Support for Famous Stars and Straps
podcast.body: Tim Armstrong of Rancid is noted for publicly wearing gear from Travis Barker's clothing company, Famous Stars and Straps, helping to promote the brand. This shows support among musicians for each other's entrepreneurial ventures. "If you look carefully, you can see Travis's gear on you guys like Tim Armstrong of Ransid".

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Operation Ivy (1987–1989) – Skacore Pioneers; Dissolved into Rancid
xref.body: Operation Ivy formed in 1987 and, like the Bosstones, embraced the blend of ska and hardcore known as skacore. They held it together for a couple of years and a couple of releases before dissolving and coalescing into a new band — Rancid, which became the first of the new wave of skacore bands to break out big. "Operation Ivy, they were formed in 1987 and like the muddy, muddy Boston's they were into that blend of Skah and Hardcore known as Skahcore."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Admiration for Rancid and Operation Ivy
xref.body: Green Day members were significant fans of both Rancid and Operation Ivy, the latter being Rancid's predecessor. Billy Joe Armstrong and Mike Dirnt frequently attended Operation Ivy shows at the renowned 924 Gilman Street punk club during their youth. "This pleased Green Day to no end because everyone in the band had been big fans of Ranset as well as Operation Ivy, Ranset's immediate ancestor. As kids, Billy Joe Armstrong and Mike Durant used to go see Op Ivy all the time at the infamous 924 Gilman Street punk club."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation of Alternative Tentacles Records
xref.body: Rather than compromise on their name or artistic vision, the Dead Kennedys decided to form their own record label, Alternative Tentacles. This label became a major influence in the Bay Area music scene and is credited with paving the way for bands like Rancid and Green Day. "So, instead of compromising the decays formed their own record label, which they called alternative tentacles."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Fourth Wave Leader
xref.body: The Interrupters, from Los Angeles, record for Hellcat Records (a label associated with Rancid) and are considered the current leader in the fourth wave of Ska. Their success marks the first female-fronted Ska hit since No Doubt. "The biggest of them all, so far, has been the Interruptors. They're from Los Angeles and record for Hellcat Records, a label associated with, and here's that name again, Ranset. This was the first female fronted SCAT hit, since no doubt. The Interruptors, the current leader in the 4th wave of SCAT."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Rock Music
xref.body: The Ramones are credited with profoundly influencing countless rock bands over several decades, with a direct lineage tracing back to their original version for bands like Rise Against, Metallica, Blink 182, Motorhead, Green Day, Guns N' Roses, The Clash, Sex Pistols, Rancid, The Pixies, The Beastie Boys, Alice in Chains, Pearl Jam, Soundgarden, The Strokes, The Offspring, and Red Hot Chili Peppers. "virtually any rock band of the last 25 years, 35 years, and you can draw a line back into the past, and that line will inevitably lead back to the Ramones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Mid-90s Punk Rock "Holy Trinity"
xref.body: The Offspring became one of three bands, alongside Green Day and Rancid, identified as the "holy trinity of punk rock" in the mid-1990s. "The offspring became part of the mid-90s holy trinity of punk rock, along with Green Day, who were also admirably filling the Kurt Cobain vacuum and Ransett, who sometimes sounded more clash than the clash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Predecessor to Rancid
xref.body: Operation Ivy was a hardcore punk band that began incorporating Ska into their sound as early as 1987. This group served as the direct predecessor to Rancid, playing a crucial role in the development of third-wave Ska. "That group was called Operation Ivy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Punk Revival Context
xref.body: Green Day was part of a larger punk revival movement in the 1990s. Their increasing popularity contributed to Rancid's ascent, as Rancid was "sucked up in their wake," demonstrating how interconnected different alt-rock revivals were. "And as punk revivalists like Green Day and the offspring got bigger and bigger, Ranset was basically sucked up in their wake."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Punk Revival Context
xref.body: The Offspring were part of the punk revival movement in the 1990s. Their growing success helped pull other bands like Rancid into the mainstream, illustrating the ripple effect of popular punk revivalists on related scenes like third-wave Ska. "And as punk revivalists like Green Day and the offspring got bigger and bigger, Ranset was basically sucked up in their wake."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Recording at Electric Lady
xref.body: Depeche Mode recorded at Electric Lady Studios in Greenwich Village, New York. "ACDC, DePesh Mode, David Bowie, Weezer, Rancid, Billy Eidle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Role in the Mid-90s Punk Revival
xref.body: Green Day emerged as the most significant band of the 1990s rock revival, playing a pivotal role in popularizing California punk and creating a "huge vortex" that drew other bands like Rancid into the mainstream. "Green Day was the biggest band of the 90s rock revival, but they were hardly the only one."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Travis Barker's Clothing Company – Famous Stars and Straps
xref.body: Travis Barker, drummer for blink-182, founded the clothing company Famous Stars and Straps in 1999, based in Corona, California. The brand targets the skate crowd and offers t-shirts, jackets, and hats for men, along with shirts, pants, and bikinis for women, in addition to accessories like belt buckles and bandanas. The company's success is bolstered by famous friends, including Tim Armstrong of Rancid, Steve-O of Sum 41, members of Avenged Sevenfold, and B-Real of Cypress Hill, who wear the brand publicly. Famous Stars and Straps generates millions in annual revenue, and its presence is notable at events like the Warped Tour. "He founded the company in 1999 and targeted the Skate Crowd."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Whipped Cream Budget for "Fight For Your Right" Video
xref.body: The music video for "(You Gotta) Fight For Your Right (To Party!)" had an "almost no budget" for the shoot. All the whipped cream used in the pie fight scene was scrounged from dumpsters behind supermarkets and was described as being "sour and rancid and smelled awful." "All the whipped cream used in the pies. It was scrounged from dumpsters behind supermarkets."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
